patient.name: Simone Clarke
patient.complaint: Painful joints, a facial rash after a sunny holiday and sharp chest pain on breathing in
background: Recurrent mouth ulcers for a year; hair thinning
Planning a pregnancy with her partner
Takes the combined pill; no other medicines

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a young woman, a photosensitive malar rash, arthralgia, ulcers and serositis; or a twist: drug-induced lupus (isoniazid), neonatal heart block (anti-Ro) or a complication such as nephritis or AIHA.

points: Simone, 26, back from two weeks in Jamaica.
A **red rash over both cheeks** since the trip.
Wrists, fingers and knees ache, both sides equally.
Sharp left chest pain, **worse on breathing in**.
Mouth ulcers keep coming back; hair falling out.

steps.lead: A young woman with a multisystem illness: think **SLE**, an immune-complex (type III) autoimmune disease.

points: Wrists tender but **no deformity** or erosions on X-ray.
Small painless palatal ulcers; patchy alopecia.
Pleural rub at the left base; tender cervical lymph nodes.

steps.lead: Simone has the malar rash, non-erosive symmetrical arthritis, mucosal ulcers, alopecia and **serositis** (pleuritis): classic multisystem SLE.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Small left pleural effusion with a clear lung: lupus pleuritis (serositis), not pneumonia.

steps.text: Serositis is a classification criterion: think pleuritis or pericarditis in a young woman.

steps.q: Simone's rash flares in the sun and spares the nasolabial folds. What is it?
steps.r: A photosensitive cheek rash sparing the **nasolabial folds** is the SLE malar rash. Seborrhoeic dermatitis typically involves the folds.

steps.lead: Simone wants a baby: her **anti-Ro/La** status matters, because these antibodies can cross the placenta and cause fetal heart block at 18-28 weeks.
Simone takes no drugs like **isoniazid**, so this is not drug-induced lupus; and her rash is malar, not discoid plaques.
Simone needs checking for every complication: **low C3/C4**, cytopenias, **haemolysis** and **lupus nephritis**, plus long-term cardiovascular risk.

steps.text: Do not pick **rheumatoid arthritis** for every symmetrical small-joint arthritis. Rash, ulcers, serositis and **non-erosive** joints point to SLE.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (urine dipstick in known SLE, ANA to rule out), 'most specific' (anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith) and how to tell a flare (ESR up, C3/C4 down) from infection (CRP up).

steps.q: Before any bloods, which bedside test must every SLE patient have?
steps.r: Every SLE patient needs a **urine dipstick** for protein and blood: lupus nephritis can be silent.

steps.title: Simone's first results
steps.text: High ESR with a near-normal CRP is the lupus pattern.

steps.lead: Simone's dipstick shows protein: a red flag for **lupus glomerulonephritis**. Her **ANA** comes back positive, so SLE cannot be ruled out.
**Anti-dsDNA** and **anti-Smith** confirm SLE. Simone's **anti-Ro** explains her photosensitivity and matters for pregnancy; a renal biopsy may follow.

visual.title: Simone's C3
visual.label: Simone 0.52
visual.caption: Complement is being consumed by immune complexes: lower C3 means more active lupus.

steps.text: **ANA** is the most **sensitive** (rule-out) test; **anti-dsDNA** and **anti-Smith** are the most **specific**. Anti-dsDNA also tracks activity and nephritis.

steps.lead: Simone's activity is tracked with anti-dsDNA, ESR and C3/C4. If she later spikes a fever with a high **CRP**, think infection before flare.

steps.text: A raised **CRP** in known SLE is not the usual flare marker. Flares raise **ESR**; a big CRP suggests **infection** (or serositis).

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': hydroxychloroquine for mild disease, azathioprine next, and high-dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate for nephritis or cerebral lupus.

steps.q: Before renal results, Simone's skin and joint disease need a long-term drug. Which is first-line?
steps.r: **Hydroxychloroquine** is the first-line DMARD for SLE. The others are for refractory or organ-threatening disease.

steps.lead: Simone starts **hydroxychloroquine** and gets a baseline eye check, because it can cause **irreversible retinopathy**.
Her painful pleuritis is a flare: a short course of **prednisolone** settles it.
If hydroxychloroquine alone had not controlled Simone's joints and skin, **azathioprine** would be the next immunosuppressant.

points: Four weeks later: ankles swollen, BP **158/96 mmHg**.

steps.lead: Simone has **lupus nephritis**: she needs **high-dose corticosteroids** plus a cytotoxic drug such as **mycophenolate** or cyclophosphamide.

steps.title: Stepping up SLE treatment
nodes: Organ involvement → methotrexate or MMF as steroid-sparing
Nephritis / cerebral lupus → high-dose steroid + cyclophosphamide or MMF
steps.caption: Organ involvement, not symptom severity, decides when to escalate.

visual.title: Simone on induction therapy
visual.caption: As treatment works, anti-dsDNA falls and C3 recovers: disease activity is settling.

steps.text: Cyclophosphamide and mycophenolate are **teratogenic**. Simone must delay pregnancy and use contraception until she is in remission on pregnancy-safe drugs.

steps.lead: Simone meets the **revised ARA/ACR classification criteria**: rash, ulcers, arthritis, serositis, renal disease, cytopenias and positive antibodies.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: which hypersensitivity type causes the nephritis, why complement falls in a flare, why anti-Ro causes fetal heart block and why drug-induced lupus spares the kidneys.

steps.lead: Simone's immune system has **lost tolerance** to her own nuclear antigens, so she makes ANA, anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith.

steps.title: From autoantibody to organ damage
nodes: Loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens
Complexes deposit in glomeruli and skin

steps.lead: Simone's kidneys, skin and pleura are all damaged the same way: **type III** immune-complex deposition activating complement.
Simone's C3 and C4 are low because complement is **used up** binding immune complexes; they rise again as she improves.
Simone's biopsy is 'full house' because whole immune complexes and complement sit along the **glomerular basement membrane**.

steps.q: Simone's anti-Ro antibody could affect a future baby. Which structure does it damage?
steps.r: Anti-Ro/La cross the placenta and cause **inflammation and fibrosis of the fetal AV node**: congenital heart block.

steps.lead: If Simone becomes pregnant, her **anti-Ro** IgG crosses the placenta, so the baby's heart rate is monitored from about 18 weeks.

visual.title: Neonatal rhythm strip (anti-Ro positive mother)
visual.caption: Complete heart block: P waves and QRS complexes are dissociated, from fibrosis of the AV node.

steps.lead: Simone's lupus is idiopathic. Drug-induced lupus produces **anti-histone** antibodies and spares the kidneys and brain, which is why it resolves on stopping the drug.

mcq.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction underlies SLE?
mcq.r: SLE is a **type III**, immune-complex mediated disease.

mcq.q: Which feature distinguishes the SLE malar rash?
mcq.r: The malar rash **spares the nasolabial folds** and is photosensitive.

mcq.q: Which antibody is the hallmark of drug-induced lupus?
mcq.r: **Anti-histone** antibodies; triggers include isoniazid, hydralazine and procainamide.

mcq.q: At what gestation does congenital heart block from anti-Ro typically appear?
mcq.r: Fetal bradycardia from anti-Ro/La appears at **18-28 weeks**.

mcq.q: Which test is the most sensitive screening (rule-out) test for SLE?
mcq.r: **ANA** is positive in over 95%; a negative ANA largely rules SLE out.

mcq.q: Which antibody correlates with disease activity and lupus nephritis?
mcq.r: **Anti-dsDNA** titres rise with activity and nephritis.

mcq.q: Which renal biopsy pattern is characteristic of lupus nephritis?
mcq.r: **'Full house'**: IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q all positive.

mcq.q: What is the major adverse effect of hydroxychloroquine?
mcq.r: **Retinal toxicity** can cause irreversible vision loss, so eyes are screened.
Cerebral lupus needs **high-dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide**.

mcq.q: Why are C3 and C4 low in active SLE?
o: Complement is consumed by immune complexes
They are lost in the urine
mcq.r: Complement is **consumed** as immune complexes form, so low C3/C4 means active disease.

prompts.q: What is SLE and who typically gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the hypersensitivity type and the patient.

points.p: Autoimmune multisystem disease
points.why: Multisystem is the clue: skin, joints, serosa, kidneys, blood, brain.

points.p: Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex)
points.why: Type II is anti-GBM (Goodpasture); type III is immune complexes.

points.p: Typically young women
points.why: Stems are usually a woman in her 20s or 30s.

prompts.q: List the classic clinical features of SLE.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem usually gives 3 or 4 of these in different systems.

points.p: Malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, photosensitive
points.why: Worse after sun exposure; a holiday is a common stem clue.

points.p: Symmetrical non-erosive arthritis or arthralgia
points.why: Non-erosive separates it from rheumatoid arthritis.

points.p: Serositis: pleuritis or pericarditis
points.why: Pleuritic chest pain in a young woman with a rash is a classic stem.

points.p: Oral, nasal or genital mucosal ulcers
points.why: Usually painless oral ulcers.

points.p: Alopecia, discoid rash, lymphadenopathy, myalgia
points.why: Constitutional and skin features complete the picture.

prompts.q: What are the haematological and renal complications of SLE?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the labs in the stem often point to one complication.

points.p: Low C3 and C4
points.why: Low complement means active disease.

points.p: Lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia
points.why: Lymphopenia is common; leucopenia does not mean infection.

points.p: AIHA: low Hb, high LDH, positive DAT (Coombs)
points.why: DAT positive means antibody-coated red cells.

points.p: Lupus nephritis: proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension, rising creatinine
points.why: Nephritic picture; check urine in every SLE patient.

points.p: Premature coronary artery disease
points.why: Long-term complication; manage risk factors.

prompts.q: How does drug-induced lupus differ from SLE, and what is discoid lupus?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a man on TB treatment with arthralgia is drug-induced lupus.

points.p: Triggered by drugs such as isoniazid (also hydralazine, procainamide)
points.why: Look for TB treatment or an old antihypertensive in the stem.

points.p: Anti-histone antibodies
points.why: The hallmark serology.

points.p: Rarely kidney or CNS involvement; resolves on stopping the drug
points.why: Management is simply stopping the drug.

points.p: Discoid lupus: red scaling plaques on sun-exposed skin
points.why: Skin-limited; can scar.

prompts.q: Which two signature presentations of SLE must you recognise?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one is in the patient's brain, the other in her baby's heart.

points.p: Neuropsychiatric (cerebral) lupus: psychosis and severe headache with malar rash
points.why: Do not call it schizophrenia when there is a malar rash.

points.p: Congenital heart block / neonatal lupus from anti-Ro and anti-La
points.why: Fetal bradycardia at 18-28 weeks.

prompts.q: What are the first-line and screening tests, and which antibodies are most specific?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: sensitive rules out, specific rules in.

points.p: Urine dipstick for proteinuria in every SLE patient
points.why: First-line: lupus nephritis can be silent.

points.p: ANA: most sensitive, positive in over 95%, rule-out test
points.why: Negative ANA makes SLE very unlikely.

points.p: Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are most specific
points.why: Anti-dsDNA also tracks activity and nephritis.

points.p: Anti-Ro: photosensitive rash, subacute cutaneous lupus, cytopenias, neonatal lupus
points.why: Check before pregnancy.

points.p: Renal biopsy: 'full house' immunofluorescence (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q)
points.why: Confirms and classifies lupus nephritis.

prompts.q: How do you monitor SLE activity, and how do you tell a flare from infection?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ESR follows lupus, CRP follows infection.

points.p: Anti-dsDNA titres rise with activity
points.why: Falling titres mean treatment is working.

points.p: ESR rises with activity
points.why: Higher ESR = more active disease.

points.p: C3/C4 fall with activity
points.why: Lower complement = more active disease.

points.p: Raised CRP suggests infection rather than flare
points.why: Flares typically do not raise CRP much.

prompts.q: What is first-line and second-line treatment for mild SLE, and the key side effect?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: mild skin and joint disease starts with one drug.

points.p: Hydroxychloroquine first-line DMARD, long-term
points.why: Used in almost every SLE patient.

points.p: Retinal toxicity: irreversible vision loss
points.why: Needs eye screening.

points.p: Azathioprine second-line if hydroxychloroquine is insufficient
points.why: Steroid-sparing immunosuppressant.

points.p: Flares: corticosteroids (prednisolone)
points.why: Short courses for flares.

prompts.q: How do you treat severe SLE: nephritis, cerebral lupus and organ-threatening flares?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: organ involvement means steroid plus a cytotoxic drug.

points.p: High-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone)
points.why: The backbone of every severe regimen.

points.p: Plus cyclophosphamide (or mycophenolate or tacrolimus) for nephritis
points.why: Cytotoxic agent needed for nephritis.

points.p: Cerebral lupus: high-dose steroids and cyclophosphamide
points.why: Neurological lupus is organ-threatening.

points.p: Methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent in severe disease with organ involvement
points.why: Also MMF, cyclophosphamide, azathioprine.

prompts.q: Explain the pathophysiology of SLE, why complement falls and why biopsy is 'full house'.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one mechanism, immune complexes, explains almost every finding.

points.p: Loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens gives ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith
points.why: Why ANA is so sensitive.

points.p: Type III: immune complexes deposit in GBM and skin
points.why: Not antibody against the GBM itself (that is type II).

points.p: Complement activated and consumed, so low C3/C4 track activity
points.why: Complement drives local inflammation.

points.p: GBM deposition gives proliferative GN with 'full house' staining
points.why: All immunoglobulin classes and complement present.

prompts.q: Why does anti-Ro cause congenital heart block, and why does drug-induced lupus spare the kidneys?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: IgG crosses the placenta; histones are the drug target.

points.p: Anti-Ro/La cross the placenta and bind fetal conduction tissue
points.why: Only IgG crosses the placenta.

points.p: Inflammation and fibrosis of the AV node
points.why: Complete heart block, often permanent.

points.p: Drugs modify histones, which become antigenic: anti-histone antibodies
points.why: Isoniazid, hydralazine, procainamide.

points.p: No renal or CNS involvement, unlike idiopathic SLE
points.why: Hence it resolves when the drug stops.

glossary.SLE: Systemic lupus erythematosus: an autoimmune, immune-complex disease affecting many organs, mostly in young women.
glossary.Type III hypersensitivity: Tissue damage caused by antigen-antibody immune complexes depositing in vessels and organs and activating complement.
glossary.Malar rash: Red butterfly-shaped rash over both cheeks and nose bridge, sparing the nasolabial folds, worse after sun.
glossary.Nasolabial folds: The creases running from the sides of the nose to the corners of the mouth.
glossary.Photosensitive: Made worse by sunlight or ultraviolet light exposure.
glossary.Discoid rash: Red, scaly, sometimes scarring plaques on sun-exposed skin; the main feature of discoid lupus.
glossary.Serositis: Inflammation of a serous lining such as the pleura (pleuritis) or pericardium (pericarditis).
glossary.Pleuritis: Inflammation of the pleura, causing sharp chest pain on breathing in and sometimes an effusion or rub.
glossary.Pleural rub: Creaking sound on auscultation as inflamed pleural layers rub together.
glossary.Non-erosive arthritis: Joint inflammation that does not destroy bone at the joint margins on X-ray, unlike rheumatoid arthritis.
glossary.Alopecia: Hair loss, often patchy or diffuse thinning in active lupus.
glossary.ANA: Antinuclear antibody: the most sensitive SLE test, positive in over 95%, so a negative result helps rule it out.
glossary.Anti-dsDNA: Antibody against double-stranded DNA; highly specific for SLE and rises with disease activity and nephritis.
glossary.Anti-Smith: Antibody against Smith nuclear protein; highly specific for SLE but less sensitive.
glossary.Anti-Ro: Anti-SSA antibody linked to photosensitive rash, cytopenias and neonatal lupus with congenital heart block.
glossary.Anti-La: Anti-SSB antibody that, with anti-Ro, can cross the placenta and cause neonatal lupus.
glossary.Anti-histone antibodies: The hallmark antibodies of drug-induced lupus.
glossary.Drug-induced lupus: Lupus-like illness caused by drugs such as isoniazid or hydralazine, sparing kidneys and brain, resolving on stopping them.
glossary.Isoniazid: Anti-tuberculosis antibiotic that can trigger drug-induced lupus.
glossary.Hydralazine: Vasodilator antihypertensive and a classic cause of drug-induced lupus.
glossary.C3: Complement component 3; falls when consumed by immune complexes, so low levels mean active lupus.
glossary.C4: Complement component 4; like C3, low levels indicate active lupus.
glossary.Complement: Blood proteins that attack pathogens and drive inflammation when activated by immune complexes.
glossary.ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: a non-specific inflammation marker that rises with SLE activity.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein: often near-normal in an SLE flare, so a high CRP suggests infection.
glossary.Lymphopenia: Low lymphocyte count, a common blood finding in active SLE.
glossary.Thrombocytopenia: Low platelet count, which can cause bruising or bleeding.
glossary.AIHA: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia: antibodies coat and destroy red cells, giving low Hb, high LDH and a positive DAT.
glossary.LDH: Lactate dehydrogenase: an enzyme released from broken cells, raised in haemolysis.
glossary.DAT: Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test: detects antibody or complement stuck to red cells.
glossary.Lupus nephritis: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis in SLE causing proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension and rising creatinine.
glossary.Full house: Renal biopsy staining positive for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q, characteristic of lupus nephritis.
glossary.Immunofluorescence: Biopsy technique using fluorescent antibodies to show which immune proteins are deposited in tissue.
glossary.GBM: Glomerular basement membrane: the filtering layer of the glomerulus where lupus immune complexes deposit.
glossary.Neonatal lupus: Lupus features in a baby caused by maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies, most seriously congenital heart block.
glossary.Congenital heart block: Complete heart block present at birth, from maternal anti-Ro/La damaging the fetal AV node.
glossary.AV node: Atrioventricular node: conducts impulses from the atria to the ventricles.
glossary.Cerebral lupus: Neuropsychiatric lupus: brain involvement causing psychosis, seizures, severe headache or confusion.
glossary.Hydroxychloroquine: Antimalarial DMARD that is first-line long-term treatment for SLE; can cause retinopathy.
glossary.Retinopathy: Damage to the retina; with hydroxychloroquine it can cause irreversible vision loss.
glossary.DMARD: Disease-modifying antirheumatic drug: a drug that controls the underlying autoimmune process, not just symptoms.
glossary.Azathioprine: Oral immunosuppressant used second-line in SLE when hydroxychloroquine is not enough.
glossary.Cyclophosphamide: Cytotoxic immunosuppressant used with high-dose steroids for lupus nephritis and cerebral lupus.
glossary.Mycophenolate mofetil: Immunosuppressant used for lupus nephritis and severe SLE; teratogenic.
glossary.MMF: Mycophenolate mofetil, an immunosuppressant used in lupus nephritis.
glossary.Tacrolimus: Calcineurin inhibitor immunosuppressant, an alternative cytotoxic option in lupus nephritis.
glossary.Steroid-sparing agent: A drug added so the steroid dose can be reduced, limiting steroid side effects.
glossary.ARA criteria: American Rheumatism Association (now ACR) classification criteria used to define SLE for diagnosis and research.

technique.stem: A 24 year old woman has a 6 week history of painful wrists and fingers on both sides and a rash on her face that worsened after a beach holiday. She has painless ulcers on her hard palate. There is an erythematous rash over both cheeks that spares the nasolabial folds. Hand X-rays show no erosions.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question in a young woman with joints plus skin: think connective tissue disease.

clues: painless ulcers on her hard palate
steps.x: Young woman, **photosensitive** rash sparing the folds (malar), mucosal ulcers, **non-erosive** arthritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Three systems involved with a malar rash: **SLE**.

elim: Dermatomyositis gives a heliotrope eyelid rash, Gottron's papules and proximal weakness.
Psoriatic arthritis has psoriasis and nail changes, often asymmetrical.
Rheumatoid arthritis is erosive and does not cause malar rash or oral ulcers.
Systemic sclerosis gives tight shiny skin, Raynaud's and dysphagia.

steps.x: **D. Systemic lupus erythematosus.** Rule: malar rash + ulcers + non-erosive arthritis = SLE.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman has fatigue, arthralgia and a photosensitive facial rash. Her antinuclear antibody is positive at a titre of 1:640. Her GP wants a test that is most specific for the suspected diagnosis.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: It asks for the most **specific** test, not the most sensitive one.
ANA positive means SLE is possible but not proven; ANA is sensitive, not specific.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Most specific SLE antibodies: **anti-dsDNA** or anti-Smith.

elim: Anti-centromere points to limited systemic sclerosis.
Anti-CCP is specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
Anti-histone is for drug-induced lupus.
Repeating the ANA adds nothing; it is sensitive, not specific.

steps.x: **C. Anti-dsDNA antibodies.** Rule: ANA rules out, anti-dsDNA/anti-Smith rule in.

technique.stem: A 31 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus takes hydroxychloroquine. She has a 2 day history of severe headache and is hearing voices. Her partner says she is agitated and paranoid. She has a malar rash. CT head and lumbar puncture are normal. She takes no other medicines.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Management of a flare with a new organ involved: the brain.

clues: CT head and lumbar puncture are normal
steps.x: Psychosis and headache with a malar rash, after infection and bleed are excluded: **cerebral lupus**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Organ-threatening lupus: **high-dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide**.

elim: Hydroxychloroquine is for mild skin and joint disease, not cerebral lupus.
Normal LP makes HSV encephalitis unlikely.
An antipsychotic alone ignores the cause.
Stopping her DMARD would not treat the flare.

steps.x: **A. High-dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide.** Rule: cerebral or renal lupus = steroid + cytotoxic.

technique.stem: A 27 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a flare with a malar rash, pleuritic chest pain and proteinuria. Her serum C3 and C4 are both low and her anti-dsDNA titre has risen.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her low complement levels?
o: Complement-binding antibody against red cells only
Loss of complement in the urine

steps.x: A mechanism question: why does complement fall in a flare?

clues: C3 and C4 are both low
steps.x: Low complement moves with rising anti-dsDNA: both reflect active immune complex disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Type III: immune complexes activate and **consume** complement.

elim: Red-cell antibodies cause AIHA, not a global fall in C3 and C4.
Hereditary deficiency would not fluctuate with flares.
Proteinuria loses albumin; it does not explain low complement.
Her liver is normal; complement is a consumption problem.

steps.x: **B. Consumption by immune complexes.** Rule: low C3/C4 = active lupus.

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman has a 2 month history of painful hands, tiredness and sharp left-sided chest pain on deep breathing. Her face became red after a holiday in Spain. She has recurrent mouth ulcers. Her temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Small left pleural effusion, lungs otherwise clear.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Photosensitive rash, ulcers, arthritis and pleuritis with an effusion, lymphopenia and high ESR but low CRP: SLE. Rheumatoid does not cause serositis with ulcers and rash.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a young woman with several systems involved.

clues: sharp left-sided chest pain on deep breathing
steps.x: Pleuritis (serositis), photosensitive rash, ulcers, arthritis; labs add lymphopenia and ESR far higher than CRP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Multisystem with serositis and a sun-worsened rash: **SLE**.

elim: Dermatomyositis gives proximal weakness and a heliotrope rash.
Rheumatoid arthritis does not cause photosensitive rash, ulcers or this lab pattern.
Sarcoidosis gives hilar nodes and erythema nodosum.
Systemic sclerosis gives tight skin and Raynaud's.

steps.x: **E. SLE.** Effusion + rash + ulcers + lymphopenia in a young woman.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has a 6 week history of aching joints and muscles and sharp chest pain on breathing in. Two months ago he started rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for pulmonary tuberculosis. He has no rash. His urine dipstick is normal. His antinuclear antibody is positive and anti-dsDNA is negative.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Arthralgia, myalgia and serositis after starting isoniazid, with normal urine and negative anti-dsDNA, is drug-induced lupus (anti-histone positive). TB pleurisy would not explain the joints and muscles.

steps.x: Diagnosis: a new multisystem illness after a new drug.

clues: sharp chest pain on breathing in
steps.x: Arthralgia, myalgia, serositis; isoniazid trigger; kidneys spared; not idiopathic SLE serology.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Drug-induced lupus**; expect anti-histone antibodies.

elim: Pyrazinamide gout causes an acute hot single joint, not myalgia and pleuritis.
Reactive arthritis follows GI or GU infection, with conjunctivitis or urethritis.
Rheumatoid arthritis does not explain pleuritic pain after a drug.
TB pleurisy does not cause polyarthralgia and myalgia with positive ANA.

steps.x: **A. Drug-induced lupus.** Rule: isoniazid + arthralgia + serositis, kidneys spared.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is 24 weeks pregnant. At a routine antenatal check the fetal heart rate is 55 bpm and regular. Fetal echocardiography shows atrioventricular dissociation with a structurally normal heart. Her lupus has been quiet on hydroxychloroquine.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of the fetal finding?
practice.e: Fetal complete heart block at 18-28 weeks in a mother with SLE is caused by transplacental anti-Ro (and anti-La). Anti-cardiolipin causes miscarriage and thrombosis, not heart block.

steps.x: A cause question: which antibody?
Fetal bradycardia from **complete heart block** in the 18-28 week window.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Neonatal lupus: **anti-Ro/La** crossing the placenta.

elim: Anti-cardiolipin (antiphospholipid) causes miscarriage, clots and pre-eclampsia.
Anti-centromere is limited systemic sclerosis.
Anti-histone is drug-induced lupus.
Anti-Smith is specific for SLE but does not damage fetal conduction.

steps.x: **D. Anti-Ro antibodies.** Rule: fetal heart block in lupus = anti-Ro/La.

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has 2 weeks of swollen ankles and frothy urine. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 164/98 mmHg. There is pitting oedema to the shins.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension and rising creatinine with low C3 and high anti-dsDNA in SLE is lupus nephritis. Minimal change has no haematuria or hypertension.

steps.x: Diagnosis of renal disease in a patient with known SLE.
Oedema, frothy urine, hypertension in SLE; labs add proteinuria, haematuria, raised creatinine, low C3, high anti-dsDNA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lupus nephritis**; biopsy would be 'full house'.

elim: Hypertensive nephropathy does not cause low C3 or high anti-dsDNA.
IgA nephropathy follows a sore throat within days, with normal complement.
Minimal change has no haematuria or hypertension and is commonest in children.
Post-streptococcal GN follows a throat infection by 2-3 weeks; no such history.

steps.x: **C. Lupus nephritis.** Rule: always dipstick SLE patients.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has 3 weeks of increasing tiredness and breathlessness on exertion. Her sclerae are yellow. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
practice.e: Low Hb with jaundice, high LDH, reticulocytosis and a positive DAT in SLE is autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. TTP is DAT negative with schistocytes and low platelets.

steps.x: Cause of anaemia in a lupus patient.
Jaundice and anaemia in SLE; labs show haemolysis (LDH, reticulocytes) that is antibody-mediated (DAT positive).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **AIHA**, a recognised SLE complication.

elim: Chronic disease anaemia is mild, with no haemolysis.
Iron deficiency is microcytic with no jaundice.
TTP is DAT negative with low platelets and schistocytes.
B12 deficiency can raise LDH but the DAT would be negative and reticulocytes low.

steps.x: **B. AIHA.** Rule: positive DAT + haemolysis in SLE.

practice.stem: A 22 year old woman is brought in by her mother with 3 days of severe headache, agitation and believing her neighbours are spying on her. She has had painful joints and a facial rash for 2 months and takes no medicines. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 130/82 mmHg. There is a rash over both cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds. Neck stiffness is absent.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: New psychosis and severe headache with arthralgia and a malar rash is cerebral (neuropsychiatric) lupus. She takes no steroids, and schizophrenia would not explain the rash and joints.

steps.x: Diagnosis: new psychosis plus a systemic illness.

clues: painful joints and a facial rash
steps.x: Psychosis + headache + malar rash + arthritis; no drugs to blame.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Neuropsychiatric (cerebral) lupus**.

elim: Meningitis gives fever, neck stiffness and a non-blanching rash.
Schizophrenia does not explain the rash and arthritis.
She takes no medicines, so not steroid-induced.
SAH is thunderclap, not 3 days of psychosis with a rash.

steps.x: **B. Neuropsychiatric lupus.** Rule: psychosis + malar rash = cerebral lupus.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has 4 months of fatigue, arthralgia of the hands and occasional mouth ulcers. She has no rash. Her GP wants to rule out systemic lupus erythematosus with a single blood test.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: ANA is positive in over 95% of SLE, so a negative result effectively rules it out. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific but miss many cases.

steps.x: The goal is to **rule out**: you need the most sensitive test.
Low suspicion; a sensitive screening test is required.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ANA**: most sensitive, rule-out test.

elim: Anti-CCP tests for rheumatoid arthritis.
Anti-dsDNA is specific but not sensitive enough to rule out.
Anti-Smith is highly specific but positive in a minority.
Rheumatoid factor is non-specific and not an SLE test.

steps.x: **D. ANA.** Rule: Sensitive rules out (ANA), specific rules in (dsDNA/Smith).

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has increasing joint pain and fatigue over 2 weeks and a returning facial rash. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. Her rheumatologist wants a blood test that best reflects lupus disease activity.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: Anti-dsDNA titres (with ESR and C3/C4) track SLE activity. ANA stays positive regardless of activity, so it is a rule-out test, not a monitoring test.

steps.x: A monitoring question: which test tracks activity?
Suspected flare; afebrile with a normal CRP, so infection is unlikely.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anti-dsDNA titre** (plus ESR, C3/C4).

elim: ANA does not reflect activity; it is the screening test.
Anti-Ro relates to skin, cytopenias and pregnancy, not activity.
Blood cultures are for suspected infection; she is afebrile with normal CRP.
Rheumatoid factor is not an SLE activity marker.

steps.x: **B. Anti-dsDNA titre.** Rule: dsDNA up, C3/C4 down = flare.

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman has just been diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus. She has a photosensitive malar rash, arthralgia of the hands and mouth ulcers. Her urine dipstick, creatinine and full blood count are normal. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
practice.e: Mild SLE (skin and joints, no organ involvement) is treated long-term with hydroxychloroquine, with eye screening for retinopathy. Cyclophosphamide is for nephritis or cerebral lupus.

steps.x: Long-term first-line treatment.

clues: urine dipstick, creatinine and full blood count are normal
steps.x: Skin and joints only: **mild** disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hydroxychloroquine**.

elim: Azathioprine is second-line if hydroxychloroquine is insufficient.
Cyclophosphamide is for organ-threatening disease.
Methotrexate is a steroid-sparing agent in more severe disease.
Rituximab is for refractory disease, not first-line.

steps.x: **C. Hydroxychloroquine.** Rule: mild SLE = hydroxychloroquine, check eyes.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has frothy urine and ankle swelling. Her BP is 156/94 mmHg and pulse rate 80 bpm. Urine protein:creatinine ratio is 310 mg/mmol and creatinine has risen from 70 to 118 µmol/L. Renal biopsy shows proliferative glomerulonephritis with 'full house' immunofluorescence.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Lupus nephritis needs high-dose corticosteroids plus a cytotoxic agent (mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide or tacrolimus). An ACE inhibitor helps proteinuria but does not treat the inflammation.

steps.x: Management of an organ-threatening complication.
Biopsy-proven **lupus nephritis** with falling renal function.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: High-dose steroid plus **cyclophosphamide, MMF or tacrolimus**.

elim: An ACE inhibitor is supportive only.
Azathioprine alone is too weak for active proliferative nephritis.
Hydroxychloroquine is for mild disease, not nephritis.
Plasma exchange is for anti-GBM disease or TTP.

steps.x: **C. High-dose steroids and MMF.** Rule: nephritis = steroid + cytotoxic.

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has taken hydroxychloroquine for 6 months. She still has painful, stiff hands and an active facial rash. She has no renal, neurological or haematological involvement. Her urine dipstick and full blood count are normal.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: If hydroxychloroquine is insufficient, the second-line immunosuppressant is azathioprine. Cyclophosphamide is reserved for serious renal, neurological or haematological disease.

steps.x: Next step after first-line failure.

clues: no renal, neurological or haematological involvement
steps.x: Mild disease not controlled by first-line; no organ threat.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Second-line: **azathioprine**.

elim: Cyclophosphamide is for serious organ involvement.
IVIG is not standard for skin and joint SLE.
Hydroxychloroquine continues; you add to it.
An NSAID alone does not control the disease.

steps.x: **A. Add azathioprine.** Rule: HCQ first, azathioprine second.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has proteinuria and haematuria. Renal biopsy shows granular deposits of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q along the glomerular basement membrane. Her serum C3 is low and anti-dsDNA high.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her renal injury?
o: Antibody binding to type IV collagen in the GBM
Direct cytotoxic T cell attack on podocytes
practice.e: Lupus nephritis is type III hypersensitivity: anti-dsDNA immune complexes deposit along the GBM and activate complement, giving granular 'full house' staining. Antibody to type IV collagen is anti-GBM disease (linear staining).

steps.x: Mechanism question: which hypersensitivity type?

clues: IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q
steps.x: Granular, all classes plus complement, complement consumed: immune complexes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Type III**: immune complex deposition with complement activation.

elim: Anti-GBM (type II) gives **linear** IgG, not granular full house.
Type IV T-cell injury does not deposit immunoglobulins.
Type I IgE reactions cause allergy, not glomerulonephritis.
Renal artery stenosis has no immune deposits.

steps.x: **D. Immune complex deposition.** Rule: SLE = type III.
